claims.text: Resistance to edge-dislocation motion is the primary mechanism governing increased hardness and strength in BCC high-entropy alloys.
The strengthening effect becomes more pronounced as edge-dislocation density increases.
Annealing can produce a BCC high-entropy alloy baseline with minimal dislocation density.
Controlled plastic deformation can increase edge-dislocation density.
Thermal treatments can be selected to increase edge-dislocation density.
Dislocation motion dominates deformation at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures within the proposed regime.
Phase transformations are negligible within the proposed temperature and strain regime.
Increasing edge-dislocation density produces more dislocation interactions and pinning.
Greater edge-dislocation interactions and pinning impede edge-dislocation motion.
Impeded edge-dislocation motion inhibits plastic deformation and thereby increases hardness and strength.
Samples with increased edge-dislocation density will have higher hardness than the annealed baseline.
Samples with increased edge-dislocation density will have higher yield strength than the annealed baseline.
The proposed behavior is limited to moderate strains and temperatures at which dislocation interactions dominate strengthening.
The proposed behavior may not hold when grain-boundary sliding or phase changes contribute strongly.
The quantitative contribution of edge dislocations relative to screw dislocations is not well defined.
The influence of chemical heterogeneity on the proposed mechanism is not well defined.
